title: Nitrogen cycle

definition.text: The biogeochemical cycle in which nitrogen changes between chemical forms as it moves among the air, land and sea.

facts.text: Its main steps are fixation, ammonification, nitrification and denitrification, carried out by both biological and physical processes.
Nitrogen gas makes up 78% of Earth's atmosphere, the largest nitrogen store, yet little of it is available to living things, so usable nitrogen is scarce in many ecosystems.
Nitrogen occurs as organic nitrogen, ammonium, nitrite, nitrate, nitrous oxide, nitric oxide and nitrogen gas; organic nitrogen sits in living organisms, humus and partly decomposed matter.
Microbes run many of the steps, either to harvest energy or to gather the nitrogen they need for growth.
Fixation is the main source of plant-available nitrogen in most ecosystems, but where bedrock is rich in nitrogen its breakdown also supplies some.
Ecologists watch the cycle closely because nitrogen supply can set the pace of primary production and decomposition.
Fossil fuel burning, synthetic nitrogen fertilizers and nitrogen in wastewater have dramatically altered the global cycle, with harm to ecosystems and human health.
The same cycle runs in the ocean, where nitrogen fixation is done mainly by cyanobacteria.

notes: A cycle diagram (fixation, ammonification, nitrification, denitrification) would teach the loop at a glance.

definition.text: The conversion of the abundant but unreactive nitrogen gas of the air into usable nitrogen compounds such as ammonia and nitrate.

facts.text: Most organisms cannot use atmospheric nitrogen because the triple bond holding its two atoms together is very strong.
Fixation happens biologically and also without life, naturally through lightning or artificially in chemical industry.
Biological fixation is catalysed by nitrogenase enzymes made by microorganisms such as cyanobacteria and rhizobia.
Lightning fixes 5 to 10 billion kg a year, but free-living or symbiotic bacteria called diazotrophs do most fixation.
Lightning-made nitrogen oxides form nitrous and nitric acids that seep into soil as nitrate plants can use.
Some diazotrophs live in symbiosis with legumes, mosses and the water fern Azolla; looser associative links occur, for example on rice roots.
About 30% of all fixed nitrogen is now made industrially by the Haber–Bosch process.
Fixation is essential to life, because DNA, proteins and other vital organic compounds all contain nitrogen.

definition.text: The enzyme complex that catalyses the reduction of nitrogen gas to ammonia in nitrogen-fixing microbes.

facts.text: It has two proteins: a catalytic iron-dependent MoFe protein and a reducing iron-only Fe protein; nitrogen is converted at a metal cluster called FeMoco.
Three forms carry molybdenum, iron or vanadium in the active site; the molybdenum form is the most common.
Each reaction uses 16 ATP and also releases hydrogen gas, making fixation energetically costly.
Oxygen rapidly destroys nitrogenase, so many bacteria stop making it when oxygen is present and cyanobacteria house it in special cells called heterocysts.

definition.text: An organism, usually a bacterium or archaeon, that can fix atmospheric nitrogen gas into usable compounds such as ammonia.

facts.text: Diazotrophs are scattered across many groups of bacteria and a few archaea; examples include rhizobia, Frankia and Azospirillum.
Because fixation costs so much energy, diazotrophs cut it back when other nitrogen sources are available and, in many species, when oxygen is high.
Symbiotic diazotrophs were long thought to matter more to the global nitrogen cycle, but free-living ones are also significant fixers.
Free-living obligate anaerobes such as Clostridium live in low-oxygen soils and decaying plant matter; methanogenic archaea also fix nitrogen in oxygen-poor soils.
Aerobic fixers such as Azotobacter vinelandii protect their nitrogenase with very high respiration rates and protective compounds.
The water fern Azolla, which harbours the cyanobacterium Anabaena, is an important green manure for rice.
On land, diazotrophs supply the nitrogen that primary producers use, and this fixed nitrogen can reduce the need for fertilizer.

title: Haber–Bosch process

definition.text: The main industrial method of making ammonia, combining nitrogen from the air with hydrogen over an iron catalyst.

facts.text: Most of its ammonia becomes nitrogen fertilizer, used directly or as ammonium nitrate and urea; in 2018 it produced about 230 million tonnes of ammonia.
In the 19th century fertilizer nitrogen came from mined niter and guano, reserves thought insufficient by 1900; air is about 78% nitrogen, but the gas is exceptionally stable.
Fritz Haber showed it working in the laboratory in 1909, Carl Bosch scaled it up for BASF, and the first industrial plant opened at Oppau in 1913.
Breaking nitrogen's triple bond is the slowest step; the catalyst needs at least 400 °C, pressures of 15–25 MPa raise the yield, and only about 15% converts per pass, so unused gases are recycled.
Most of its hydrogen comes from natural gas, and it uses 1–2% of the world's energy and causes about 3% of global carbon dioxide emissions.
It now makes about 30% of all fixed nitrogen, and fertilizer production is the largest human source of fixed nitrogen on land.
Nearly 50% of the nitrogen in human tissues comes from it, and it enabled world population to grow from 1.6 billion in 1900 to 7.7 billion by November 2018.

It is one of the largest contributors to reactive nitrogen in the biosphere; with nitrogen use efficiency typically under 50%, runoff causes nitrate leaching and eutrophication, and cheap fertilizer discourages legume rotations.

definition.text: The nineteenth-century research showing that living organisms, above all bacteria, fix nitrogen from the air.

facts.text: Jean-Baptiste Boussingault discovered biological nitrogen fixation in 1838.
Experiments in 1855 and 1887 had shown that nitrogen did not enter plants directly from the air.
Hermann Hellriegel and Hermann Wilfarth found the role of nitrogen-fixing bacteria in 1886–1888, opening a new era of soil science.
In 1901 Martinus Beijerinck showed that Azotobacter chroococcum fixes atmospheric nitrogen; it was the first known diazotroph.

conflicts.text: Hellriegel and Wilfarth discovered the process in 1880.
conflicts.note: Same page gives 1880 for the Hellriegel–Wilfarth discovery.

conflicts.text: Symbiotic fixation was discovered by Hellriegel and Wilfarth in 1887.
conflicts.note: A quoted source on the same page gives 1887.

title: Ammonification

definition.text: The conversion by bacteria and fungi of organic nitrogen in dead organisms and wastes into ammonia or ammonium.

facts.text: When a plant or animal dies, or an animal excretes waste, its nitrogen is organic, in forms such as amino acids and DNA.
Ammonification is also called nitrogen mineralization and is the last step of the cycle that involves organic compounds.
Many enzymes take part, including dehydrogenases, proteases and deaminases.
Rates rise with soil organic nitrogen, microbial biomass and annual precipitation, and respond closely to temperature.
It slows under vegetation with a high carbon-to-nitrogen ratio and when sugar is added to the soil.
Together with nitrification it makes up mineralization, the complete breakdown of organic material into mineral nitrogen.
In waterlogged peat, organic matter decomposing without oxygen still yields ammonium by ammonification.

notes: Mineralization (soil science) is the organic-matter chapter's seed and covers mineralization of all elements; this entry is the nitrogen step only.

definition.text: The uptake of nitrate or ammonium by plants and microbes and its incorporation into their own organic compounds.

facts.text: Plants take up nitrate or ammonium from the soil through their root hairs.
Absorbed nitrate is reduced first to nitrite and then to ammonium before it is built into amino acids, nucleic acids and chlorophyll.
Plants with rhizobia receive some nitrogen straight from the nodules, partly as amino acids exchanged with the bacteria.
Many bacteria and other heterotrophs can use inorganic compounds such as ammonium as their only nitrogen source.

title: Denitrification

definition.text: The microbial reduction of nitrate, through a series of gaseous nitrogen oxides, to nitrogen gas.

facts.text: Facultative anaerobic bacteria use it as a form of respiration, breathing nitrate instead of oxygen while oxidizing an electron donor such as organic matter.
Nitrate is reduced step by step to nitrite, nitric oxide and nitrous oxide before ending as nitrogen gas, completing the nitrogen cycle.
It needs very low oxygen, below 10%, plus an electron donor such as organic carbon, hydrogen gas or reduced sulfur, so it thrives in waterlogged soils.
The nitrogen gas it releases is inert and unavailable to plants, so denitrification removes nitrogen from the soil.
It can leak nitrous oxide, an ozone-depleting greenhouse gas with a considerable influence on global warming.
Soil pH and texture moderate the process, and higher pH drives it closer to completion as nitrogen gas rather than nitrous oxide.
A carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of 2:1 can support full nitrate reduction regardless of temperature or carbon source.
Because it removes nitrate and so cuts leaching to groundwater, it is used to treat sewage and high-nitrogen animal wastes.

notes: Denitrifying bacteria (seed, chunk 03) is the organism entry; this one is the process, from the crawled Denitrification article.

title: Dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium

definition.text: An anaerobic respiration in which microbes oxidize organic matter using nitrate instead of oxygen, reducing it to nitrite and then to ammonium; also called nitrate ammonification.

facts.text: Unlike denitrification, which turns nitrate into nitrogen gas lost to the system, it keeps nitrogen bioavailable as soluble ammonium; the two groups of microbes compete for nitrate.

A periplasmic nitrate reductase performs the first step and cytochrome c nitrite reductase the second, so only organisms with the nrf gene can carry it out; some nitrous oxide may still be released, more at higher pH.
It usually makes up about 15% of total nitrate reduction, and it is favoured where organic carbon is plentiful relative to nitrate, such as organic matter with a high C/N ratio.
It is most common in prokaryotes but also occurs in eukaryotic microorganisms, and it is part of both the terrestrial and oceanic nitrogen cycles.

notes: Gap-fill: re-anchored from Nitrogen cycle#Dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium to the crawled DNRA article (mostly marine; the 15% share comes from its Marine context section).

definition.text: Complete ammonia oxidation: nitrification carried out entirely by one organism, which turns ammonia into nitrite and then nitrate.

facts.text: Nitrification was long thought to need two groups, ammonia oxidizers making nitrite and nitrite oxidizers making nitrate.
A single complete nitrifier was predicted in 2006 and found in 2015 in the genus Nitrospira, prompting an update to the nitrogen cycle.
The complete oxidation yields more energy (−349 kJ per mol of ammonia) than ammonia oxidation (−275 kJ) or nitrite oxidation (−74 kJ) alone.
Comammox occurs in freshwater and terrestrial ecosystems and in water-treatment systems, but its genes are not abundant in the oceans.

definition.text: Anaerobic ammonium oxidation: a microbial process that turns ammonium and nitrite directly into nitrogen gas and water.

facts.text: It is carried out by bacteria of the phylum Planctomycetota, first identified in 1999, inside a membrane-bound compartment called the anammoxosome.
Unlike denitrification it needs no organic carbon, using ammonium and nitrite directly.
It occurs in freshwater lakes, riverbanks and agricultural soils such as rice paddies, and releases less nitrous oxide than denitrification.
It may account for 30–50% of the nitrogen lost from the ocean.

verification.title: The Anammoxosome Organelle Is Crucial for the Energy Metabolism of Anaerobic Ammonium Oxidizing Bacteria
verification.evidence: Now, anammox bacteria are recognized as major players in the global nitrogen cycle and estimated to be responsible for up to 50% of the nitrogen in the air that we breathe.
verification.note: the paper's up to 50% is anammox's share of atmospheric nitrogen; the entry gives its share of nitrogen lost from the ocean (30-50%)

definition.text: The biological oxidation of ammonia to nitrate, by way of nitrite.

facts.text: It is an important step of the nitrogen cycle in soil, carried out aerobically by small groups of autotrophic bacteria and archaea.
Nitrifiers are chemoautotrophs: they draw energy from both oxidation steps and take their carbon from carbon dioxide.
In the first step, nitritation, ammonia-oxidizing bacteria and archaea turn ammonia or ammonium into nitrite; this is usually the rate-limiting step.
In the second step, nitratation, nitrite-oxidizing bacteria turn nitrite into nitrate; in comammox bacteria one organism does both steps.
Soil nitrification rates depend on ammonium supply, aeration, soil moisture, a near-neutral pH and temperature.
Soil's net negative charge holds ammonium tightly but not nitrate, so turning fertilizer ammonia into nitrate increases leaching to groundwater.
Nitrification also releases nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas about 300 times more potent than carbon dioxide that contributes 6% of greenhouse warming.
Liming raises soil biological activity and fertility, in particular by increasing nitrification.

definition.text: Chemolithotrophic bacteria that get their energy by oxidizing ammonia or nitrite, including the genera Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter and Nitrospira.

facts.text: They come in two types: ammonia-oxidizing bacteria, which make nitrite, and nitrite-oxidizing bacteria, which make nitrate; the two groups grow together.
Ammonia oxidizers belong to the Betaproteobacteria and Gammaproteobacteria; nitrite oxidizers to the Nitrospinota, Nitrospirota, Pseudomonadota and Chloroflexota.
Key enzymes on their internal membranes are ammonia monooxygenase, hydroxylamine oxidoreductase and nitrite oxidoreductase.
They are most numerous where ammonia is plentiful, such as sites of heavy protein decomposition and sewage treatment plants.
In soil, ammonia oxidizers convert ammonia from decomposing organic matter or fertilizer into nitrite, which nitrite oxidizers then use.
Soil genera include Nitrosospira, an ammonia oxidizer, and Nitrobacter and Nitrospira, nitrite oxidizers.
Sergei Winogradsky described the two-step process in 1890.

definition.text: A genus of Gram-negative bacteria that oxidize ammonia to nitrite, one of five genera of ammonia-oxidizing bacteria.

facts.text: As an obligate chemolithoautotroph it uses ammonia for energy and carbon dioxide for carbon, and needs oxygen.
Its enzymes ammonia monooxygenase and hydroxylamine oxidoreductase turn ammonia into nitrite; when oxygen is low, nitrous oxide and nitric oxide form as by-products.
It thrives at pH 6.0–9.0 and 20–30 °C where ammonia is abundant, and occurs in fertilized soils.
On farms its nitrification can lead to leaching and lost nitrogen, which inhibitors limit; in wastewater plants it is used to remove nitrogen.

definition.text: Archaea, mainly of the group Nitrososphaerota, that carry out the first step of nitrification by oxidizing ammonia to nitrite.

facts.text: Until they were found in 2005, ammonia-oxidizing bacteria were thought to be the only organisms that could oxidize ammonia.
They outnumber ammonia-oxidizing bacteria in both soils and marine environments, so they may contribute more to ammonia oxidation there.
Crenarchaeol, a lipid thought to be made only by these archaea, has been proposed as a biomarker for them.

title: Nitrification inhibitor

definition.text: A chemical added with ammonia, ammonium or urea fertilizers to slow their conversion to nitrate in the soil.

facts.text: Also called nitrogen stabilizers, they keep nitrogen as ammonium rather than nitrate, an anion more prone to leaching.
They work mainly by suppressing the bacteria that oxidize ammonia, typically by binding the active site of the enzyme ammonia monooxygenase.
Common inhibitors include dicyandiamide, ammonium thiosulfate and nitrapyrin.
They are added to about 50% of the fall-applied anhydrous ammonia in US states such as Illinois.
They usually raise fertilizer nitrogen recovery in row crops, but benefits depend on conditions and show most at less than optimal nitrogen rates.
Environmental concerns add to their appeal, because nitrification yields nitrate that leaches to groundwater and nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas.
Some, such as nitrapyrin, also suppress methane oxidation by methanotrophic bacteria.

notes: S:09d69b1386bf says some inhibitors 'inhibit the production of methane', while S:5cdc74fd5382 and S:d3fd3fd7bdc4 say they suppress methane oxidation; the methane fact follows the latter two.

definition.text: The late nineteenth-century work that proved nitrification is carried out by microbes in two steps.

facts.text: Louis Pasteur first suggested in 1862 that oxidizing ammonia to nitrate is a biological process.
In 1877 Schloesing and Müntz proved it microbial using sewage and sterilized sand; Robert Warington confirmed this in garden soil at Rothamsted in 1878.
Warington first observed in 1879 that nitrification has two steps, which John Munro confirmed in 1886.
Percy and Grace Frankland probably isolated the first pure ammonia-oxidizing culture in 1890; Sergei Winogradsky succeeded in 1891.

title: Soil nitrous oxide emissions

definition.text: The release of nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas, from soils as a by-product of microbial nitrification and denitrification.

facts.text: Microbial routes include autotrophic nitrification, heterotrophic denitrification, nitrifier denitrification, fungal denitrification and non-biological chemodenitrification.
Output depends on mineral nitrogen and organic matter supply, acidity, soil type, soil temperature and water content.
Soils under natural vegetation give 60% of naturally produced nitrous oxide.
Fertilized farm soils and livestock manure make up 42% of human nitrous oxide emissions, and runoff and leaching of fertilizers another 25%.
Cultivation, nitrogen fertilizers and animal waste handling stimulate soil bacteria to produce more nitrous oxide.
Emissions are hard to measure because most of a year's output can come in short 'hot moments' or at small 'hotspots'.
Nitrous oxide is the third most important greenhouse gas for warming and a major ozone-depleting substance.
Modest biochar additions to soil can cut nitrous oxide emissions by up to 80%.

notes: No crawled page is devoted to soil N2O; anchored on the Nitrous oxide section on its biological sources, with support from Fertilizer, Denitrification, Nitrification and Biochar sentences.

definition.text: A diverse group of bacteria from many phyla that carry out denitrification, reducing nitrate to nitrogen gases.

facts.text: They are widespread in soils and sediments and use nitrate and nitrite in place of oxygen as the final electron acceptor.
Over 50 genera and 125 species are known, making up an estimated 10–15% of the bacteria in water, soil and sediment.
Most are facultative aerobic heterotrophs, such as species of Pseudomonas, Alcaligenes and Bacillus, that switch to nitrate when oxygen runs out.
Four enzymes act in turn: nitrate reductase, nitrite reductase, nitric oxide reductase and nitrous oxide reductase, which yields nitrogen gas.
Their reducing power comes from organic carbon (heterotrophic denitrification) or from hydrogen, reduced iron or sulfur (autotrophic denitrification).
By sending nitrogen back to the atmosphere they lower soil fertility, and their by-products include nitric oxide and the greenhouse gas nitrous oxide.
In one soil, the drilosphere, the soil shaped by earthworms, held 16 per cent of the denitrifiers.
Wastewater plants use them after nitrification, feeding them organic carbon in an oxygen-free basin so nitrate bubbles off as nitrogen gas.

title: Denitrification-coupled methane oxidation
article: Denitrifying bacteria#Anaerobic oxidation of methane coupled to denitrification

definition.text: The anaerobic oxidation of methane by denitrifying bacteria that use the electrons to reduce nitrate, removing both methane and fixed nitrogen.

facts.text: It was first observed in 2008 and works in habitats from sediments to peat bogs and stratified water columns.
It can remove excess nitrate from fertilizer runoff even under hypoxic conditions.
In deep lakes such as Lake Constance, this nitrate-dependent process, carried out by Methylomirabilis oxyfera-like bacteria, is a dominant methane sink.

definition.text: The conversion of inorganic nutrients into organic compounds by microbes or plants, which makes them unavailable to plants; the opposite of mineralization.

facts.text: Soil bacteria take up inorganic nitrogen and build it into amino acids and other large biological molecules.
Immobilization and mineralization run side by side, steadily shifting decomposing nitrogen between organic and inorganic states.
Which one wins depends on the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of the plant residues being decomposed.
Above a C:N ratio of about 30:1, microbes draw on mineral nitrogen such as nitrate; below about 25:1, decomposition releases surplus nitrogen.
Ploughing in high-carbon materials such as sawdust or straw stimulates microbes, raises their nitrogen demand and causes immobilization.
Microbes out-compete plants for ammonium and nitrate during immobilization, so crops can easily become nitrogen deficient.
As decomposition releases carbon dioxide the ratio falls, and once it is nearly complete soil mineral nitrogen ends higher than at the start.
Nitrogen is immobilized in two ways: in microbial biomass and in the by-products of microbial activity.

definition.text: All forms of nitrogen in the environment except unreactive nitrogen gas, also called fixed nitrogen.

facts.text: Because nitrogen gas is so unreactive, it must be fixed into other forms before living things can use it for growth.
Breaking the strong triple bond of nitrogen gas to make reactive nitrogen takes a large amount of energy, 226 kcal per mole.
Common forms are nitrogen oxide gases, ammonia, nitrous oxide and nitrate; ammonium salts, urea and nitrate are also fertilizer components.
Soil bacteria and archaea fix nitrogen gas mainly into ammonia, some of them in symbiosis with legumes.
Just over half of all reactive nitrogen entering the biosphere now comes from human activity such as industrial fertilizer production.
Denitrification eventually returns reactive nitrogen to nitrogen gas, but an excess can cause problems such as eutrophication.
Because every form enters the nitrogen cycle, excess reactive nitrogen spreads quickly through the environment and its problems must be tackled together.

title: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle
article: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle

definition.text: The large changes people have made to the global nitrogen cycle, chiefly through synthetic fertilizer and fossil fuel burning.

facts.text: Agricultural and industrial nitrogen inputs now exceed natural nitrogen fixation, largely because of Haber–Bosch fertilizers and fossil fuel combustion.
Growing legumes, making fertilizer and burning fuels has more than doubled the yearly transfer of nitrogen into biologically available forms.
Until 1850, natural and legume-driven fixation and added organic matter were farming's only nitrogen sources; the Haber–Bosch process became the largest fertilizer source after the 1950s.
From 1890 to 1990, human-made reactive nitrogen rose almost ninefold while the human population more than tripled.
In farm soils, fertilizer has boosted nitrification and denitrification, both of which leak nitric oxide and nitrous oxide.
As ammonium accumulates, nitrification releases hydrogen ions that acidify the soil, and mobile nitrate leaches out with calcium and magnesium.
Human activities produce 35% of global nitrous oxide emissions, about 20% from agriculture such as fertilizer use and manure management.
Excess fertilizer nitrogen is a significant source of nitrate pollution in groundwater and surface water.

conflicts.text: Generation of reactive nitrogen has increased over 10 fold in the past century.
conflicts.note: Nitrogen cycle page; the ninefold figure covers 1890–1990, so the windows differ in end year.

conflicts.text: About 40% of N2O emissions are from humans.
conflicts.note: Nitrous oxide page gives about 40% (2007–2016 budget) against 35% here.

notes: S:3c81c8e8b838 says global Nr creation rose nearly 50% between 1600 and 1990, hard to square with the ninefold (1890-1990) and tenfold (past century) figures for human-made Nr; worth a check.

title: Nitrogen deposition
article: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle#Biosphere

definition.text: The fall of reactive nitrogen from the atmosphere onto land and water, in rain, as gases or as aerosols.

facts.text: It arrives as nitrate, ammonium and organic nitrogen in precipitation, as ammonia and nitric acid gases, or as ammonium nitrate aerosols.
Increased deposition can acidify soils, streams and lakes and alter forest and grassland productivity; grasslands gain at first, then decline past critical thresholds.
Extra nitrogen favours fast-growing plants that shade out slower ones, lowering species richness; on nitrogen-poor heathland, invading grasses replace heath.
Ammonia and ammonium can harm plants adapted to using nitrate, causing poor root and shoot growth.

title: Nitrogen saturation
article: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle#Impacts on productivity and nutrient cycling

definition.text: The state in which available nitrogen exceeds what vegetation, soil and microbes can take up, so the excess is lost to water and air.

facts.text: Added nitrogen is often rapidly immobilized by microbes at first; what remains depends on how much the plant community can absorb.
Studies report both positive and negative effects of nitrogen deposition on forest growth and carbon storage; long-term additions undercut the idea that extra nitrogen raises carbon sequestration.
Saturation can upset nutrient balance, for example through calcium lost with leaching nitrate, and may lead to forest decline.
A 15-year nitrogen-addition study at Harvard Forest found more leaching, higher pine mortality and an end to biomass accumulation.

contested_note: Sources disagree on whether added nitrogen raises forest productivity and carbon storage or, past saturation, causes decline.

title: Nitrogen cascade
article: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle#Integration

definition.text: The sequential passage of the same reactive nitrogen from one ecosystem to the next, causing effects at each step.

facts.text: Some systems store reactive nitrogen along the way, delaying the cascade and intensifying its local effects.
Most reactive nitrogen applied to farmland cascades through air, water and land until denitrification turns it back into nitrogen gas.
The final microbial step to nitrogen gas matters because the atmosphere is the ultimate sink for reactive nitrogen.
Managed buffer strips and wetlands can remove much of the nitrate leaving farms by denitrification, damping the cascade.

title: Phosphorus cycle

definition.text: The biogeochemical cycle that moves phosphorus through rocks, water and living things.

facts.text: Unlike many cycles it has almost no gas phase, so it is studied mainly as the movement of orthophosphate through land and water.
Living things need phosphorus for DNA, RNA, ATP and cell-membrane phospholipids; plants take it up as phosphate and build it into organic compounds.
Phosphate moves quickly through plants and animals but very slowly through soil and ocean, making this one of the slowest biogeochemical cycles.
Over geological time it is driven by tectonic uplift and weathering of phosphate rock such as apatite, the main source of bioavailable phosphorus on land.
Short-term changes in soil are chemical and biological, and soil microorganisms act as both sinks and sources of available phosphorus.
Low soil phosphorus slows both plant growth and the growth of soil microbes.
Soil phosphorus washes to rivers and lakes and on to the ocean, where only about 1% of what sinks to the deep sea is buried in sediments.
Phosphates from fertilizers, sewage and detergents can over-enrich lakes and streams; freshwater algal blooms are generally caused by excess phosphorus.

distinct_from: Human impact on the phosphorus cycle

title: Phosphorus release by weathering

definition.text: The slow freeing of phosphate from minerals such as apatite as rocks weather, the main natural source of phosphorus on land.

facts.text: The rate at which weathering releases phosphorus limits how much an ecosystem has, and apatite dissolution is a key control on productivity.
Apatite, the main primary phosphorus mineral, breaks down by carbonation.
Little of the released phosphorus reaches living things, because it mostly reacts with other soil minerals.
As weathering and soil development advance, phosphorus precipitates into insoluble forms and becomes unavailable, so over thousands of years land loses available phosphorus.
Available phosphorus cycles biologically in the upper soil, while deeper phosphorus is mostly tied up in reactions with secondary minerals.
Dust storms carry phosphorus-bearing particles of weathered rock far afield; dust from northern Africa is thought to help sustain the Amazon rainforest.

distinct_from: Human impact on the phosphorus cycle

title: Soil phosphorus retention

definition.text: The binding of phosphate by soil minerals, by adsorption or precipitation, which keeps dissolved phosphorus low and limits what plants can take up.

facts.text: Phosphate is adsorbed onto iron and aluminium oxyhydroxides in acidic soils and precipitates onto calcite in neutral to calcareous soils.
This retention is usually seen as the most important control on how much phosphorus is available in mineral soil.
Much of the soluble phosphate applied as fertilizer is immobilized rapidly and becomes unavailable to plants.
Plants and microbes use special strategies to gather phosphorus from the low concentrations left in soil solution.
Phosphorus-starved bacteria release iron-binding molecules and may dissolve iron minerals to reach the phosphate adsorbed on them.
Waterlogging can make a poorly drained soil reducing within 7–10 days, sharply raising dissolved phosphorus and the risk of it leaching.

distinct_from: Human impact on the phosphorus cycle
notes: Often called phosphorus fixation; no crawled page of its own. Anchored on the Phosphorus cycle section that states the adsorption and precipitation mechanism.

title: Organic phosphorus mineralization

definition.text: The breakdown of organic phosphorus compounds by enzymes into free phosphate that plants and microbes can use.

facts.text: Phosphatases, nucleases and phytase are among the enzymes that release phosphate from organic matter.
Enzymatic hydrolysis of organic phosphorus is an essential step for plant and microbial nutrition and for moving organic phosphorus from soil to water.
Plant growth depends on rapid root uptake of the phosphorus released from dead organic matter.
Soil phosphatase activity can serve as an indicator of phosphorus mineralization potential and availability.

distinct_from: Human impact on the phosphorus cycle

title: Human impact on the phosphorus cycle

definition.text: The changes people have made to the phosphorus cycle, chiefly by mining phosphate rock for fertilizer.

facts.text: About 110 teragrams of phosphorus have been added to the environment since mining spread in the 1840s; from 1900 to 2022 global mining rose 72-fold.
Most mined phosphorus becomes fertilizer, and at current rates the geological system cannot replace what is taken.
Repeated excess applications of liquid hog manure harm the cycle, and biosolids can raise available soil phosphorus.
Over the last 40 years the N:P ratio has risen from 19:1 to 30:1, leaving phosphorus less available to ecosystems.

definition.text: Beneficial soil bacteria that dissolve inorganic phosphate from insoluble compounds, making it available to plants.

facts.text: They release low-molecular-weight organic acids whose hydroxyl and carboxyl groups chelate the cations bound to phosphate, turning it soluble.
Roots and other microbes release similar organic acids, and mycorrhizal fungi produce oxalic acid, freeing phosphorus held by aluminium, iron and calcium.
Phosphate solubilization by rhizosphere microbes is considered one of the most important traits for plant phosphate nutrition.
Used as a biofertilizer, seed inoculation can give yield responses equal to 30 kg/ha P2O5, or 50 percent of the need for phosphatic fertilizer.

title: Sulfur cycle

definition.text: The biogeochemical cycle in which sulfur moves between rocks, waters and living things, changing its oxidation state as it goes.

facts.text: Sulfur is an essential element of many proteins and cofactors, and its compounds serve as oxidants or reductants in cellular respiration.
Its oxidation state ranges from +6 in sulfate to −2 in sulfides, so elemental sulfur can either give or take electrons.
Decomposition mineralizes organic sulfur to hydrogen sulfide, elemental sulfur and sulfide minerals, much as deamination releases nitrogen.
Sulfur oxidizers turn sulfide and elemental sulfur into sulfate, and sulfate reducers turn sulfate back into sulfide.
Plants, fungi and many prokaryotes take up sulfate and reduce it to build their own sulfur compounds.
Left alone, sulfur stays in rocks for millions of years until uplift, erosion and weathering release it; most sulfur sits in seawater and sedimentary rocks, not living things.

distinct_from: Human impact on the sulfur cycle

title: Microbial sulfur oxidation

definition.text: The oxidation of reduced sulfur compounds, such as sulfide and elemental sulfur, by microorganisms that gain energy from it, often to fix carbon.

facts.text: Aerobic sulfide oxidizers are usually autotrophs that use the energy from sulfide or elemental sulfur to fix carbon dioxide.
Intermediates include elemental sulfur and thiosulfate; at low oxygen, microbes stop at elemental sulfur and store it as globules.
Photosynthetic green and purple sulfur bacteria and some chemolithotrophs oxidize hydrogen sulfide to elemental sulfur.
Key genera include Thiobacillus and Acidithiobacillus; oxygen or nitrate accepts the electrons, and some bacteria and archaea oxidise elemental sulfur all the way to sulfuric acid.

distinct_from: Human impact on the sulfur cycle
notes: Re-anchored on the dedicated page Microbial oxidation of sulfur (marine-focused); biological oxidation far exceeds chemical oxidation of sulfide in most environments (S:7625795101c0).

title: Dissimilatory sulfate reduction
article: Sulfur cycle#Biologically and thermochemically driven sulfate reduction

definition.text: The reduction of sulfate to hydrogen sulfide by sulfate-reducing microbes, which use sulfate in place of oxygen to oxidize organic compounds.

facts.text: Sulfate can also be reduced without microbes at high temperature (thermochemical reduction); both routes give hydrogen sulfide, carbon dioxide, carbonates, sulfur and metal sulfides.
Organic acids are the main compounds that bacterial sulfate reducers oxidize.
Under reducing conditions, sulfate-reducing bacteria turn the sulfate of gypsum back into sulfide, and they deposit pyrite in sediments.
Martinus Beijerinck isolated the first known sulfate-reducing bacterium, now Desulfovibrio desulfuricans.

distinct_from: Human impact on the sulfur cycle

title: Human impact on the sulfur cycle

definition.text: The large rise in sulfur flowing through air, water and soil since people began burning coal and other fossil fuels.

facts.text: Mining coal and extracting petroleum mobilizes 150 × 10^12 g of sulfur a year, more than double the rate of 100 years ago.
Sulfur dioxide emitted as pollution forms sulfuric acid, which can drop rain pH to 4.3 or lower; sulfate deposition has risen 30-fold over the most polluted areas.
As controls on acid rain cut atmospheric sulfur inputs, sulfur deficiency has become widespread in many European countries.
Sulfur is therefore increasingly added to fertilizers, and heavy nitrogen fertilizing on low-sulfur fields can cause sulfur deficiency by dilution.

definition.text: The biogeochemical cycle that moves potassium through Earth's rocks, soils, living things, air and waters.

facts.text: With nitrogen and phosphorus, potassium is one of the three major nutrients plants need in large amounts; it controls the opening of stomata.
Potassium makes up 2.6% of Earth's crust, held in feldspar, biotite and muscovite; chemical weathering supplies up to 11% of plant demand.
Some plants and bacteria release organic acids that make soil potassium accessible, and plants can 'pump' potassium from deeper layers to the surface.
Potassium is the most abundant ion in plant cells, and returns to the soil as plant matter decays.
It leaches from plants faster than nitrogen or phosphorus because it exists only as the small soluble K+ ion.
Crops remove potassium faster than weathering replaces it, so about 28 Tg of the 32 Tg mined each year goes onto fields, mostly as potassium chloride (potash).
Leaving crop residues to decay on fields returns their potassium and limits depletion; at current use, K2O reserves are expected to last 100 years.
Leaching and erosion carry 1400 Tg of potassium a year to groundwater, rivers and oceans; the hydrosphere is the largest potassium reservoir.

definition.text: The three forms in which soil holds potassium: fixed in minerals, exchangeable on particle surfaces, and dissolved in soil solution.

facts.text: Fixed potassium, locked in feldspar, mica and illite, makes up 96–99% of soil potassium.
Exchangeable potassium, adsorbed on clay particles and organic matter, makes up 1–2%.
Potassium in soil solution is the form plants absorb most readily, but it is only 0.1–0.2% of the total.
Soil potassium is most concentrated in the uppermost layers.

definition.text: The transfer of calcium between dissolved and solid forms as it moves through rocks, soils, waters and living things.

facts.text: Calcium is stored in rocks mainly as calcium carbonate or calcium silicate, in minerals such as calcite, dolomite, phosphate and gypsum.
Rocks slowly dissolve and release calcium ions; calcium minerals weather more easily than magnesium minerals, so waters are richer in calcium.
Calcium held as lime is unusable by plants until carbonic acid, formed from carbon dioxide and water, dissolves it, faster for small particles than large rocks.
Lime leached into soil raises calcium, stabilizes pH and supplies soluble Ca2+ ions that roots can absorb.
In plants, calcium rises in the xylem with water and, as calcium pectate, stiffens cell walls; it also helps enzymes signal growth.
Released calcium helps soil microorganisms reach phosphorus and other micronutrients.
When plants and animals die, decomposers return their calcium to the soil; fertilizers have also raised soil calcium.
In the ocean, shell-building organisms turn dissolved calcium into calcium carbonate, its main marine sink and the origin of limestone.

title: Biogeochemical cycle

definition.text: The movement and transformation of chemical elements and compounds between living things, the atmosphere, water and Earth's crust, including the soil.

facts.text: Energy flows one way through ecosystems, entering as sunlight and leaving as heat, but the matter of living things is conserved and recycled.
Major cycles include those of carbon, nitrogen and water; others cover oxygen, hydrogen, phosphorus, calcium, iron and sulfur.
Carbon, nitrogen, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur, the main elements of organic molecules, can persist for long periods in air, land, water or rock.
Each cycle runs through the biotic compartment, the biosphere, and the abiotic ones: atmosphere, lithosphere and hydrosphere.
Microorganisms drive much of the cycling; without them many of the processes would not happen at all.
The cycles are interconnected and help regulate climate and support plant growth and ecosystem health.
Burning fossil fuels and heavy fertilizer use can disrupt the cycles, contributing to climate change and pollution.

notes: S:7ea07521841a (lead) says plants convert atmospheric nitrogen by nitrogen fixation, whereas the nitrogen pages credit microbes (diazotrophs); not used here, worth a verification look.

definition.text: The places where elements are held during a cycle: long-term reservoirs and short-term exchange pools, with residence time measuring how long an element stays.

facts.text: A reservoir holds a chemical for a long time, as coal deposits store carbon.
Exchange pools such as plants and animals hold elements only briefly before releasing them back to the air or surroundings.
Reservoirs are generally abiotic, while exchange pools are generally biotic.
Residence time, also called turnover time, is how long a chemical is held in one place.

definition.text: The biogeochemical cycle of iron, chiefly its cycling between the +2 (ferrous) and +3 (ferric) oxidation states.

facts.text: Iron is an essential micronutrient, part of hemoglobin, the nitrogenase enzymes of nitrogen fixation and the ferredoxin of electron transport.
Ferric iron is the stable form where oxygen is present but dissolves poorly, so although abundant in the crust, iron is a limiting nutrient in most regions.

Iron-oxidizing bacteria turn soluble ferrous iron into insoluble ferric iron, while bacteria such as Shewanella and Geobacter, without oxygen, reduce ferric iron to the more bioavailable ferrous form.
Ferric hydroxides bind phosphorus, which is released when anoxic microbes reduce the iron; ferrous iron can also reduce nitrate, linking iron to the nitrogen cycle.

title: Bioavailability (soil)

definition.text: The amount of an element or compound in soil that an organism can actually take up across its cell membranes.

facts.text: In environmental and farm use the term mostly concerns contaminants such as organic pollutants and heavy metals, for example when judging the risk of spreading sewage sludge.
Roots and soil organisms take up almost only dissolved substances; sorbed or precipitated forms must re-dissolve in the soil solution before they become available.
Soil pH, ion exchange capacity, organic matter, texture and porosity all shape it; soils with more exchange capacity and organic matter adsorb more and so show lower bioavailability.
Bioavailability falls the longer a contaminant stays in contact with soil, an effect called ageing caused by diffusion and sorption.

notes: Assigned by the concept graph; the page leans toward contaminants, so the contamination chapter may also cite it.

definition.text: The movement and exchange of inorganic and organic matter back into the production of living matter, also called ecological recycling.

facts.text: Energy flows one way through ecosystems, but mineral nutrients cycle; the cycles include those of carbon, sulfur, nitrogen, water, phosphorus and oxygen.
Textbooks often treat it as a synonym of biogeochemical cycle, but the term usually means cycling within an ecosystem as a unit, linked to the larger global cycles by inputs and outputs.
Recycling is regulated largely during decomposition; cellulose-degrading enzymes, for example, recycle plant material.
Some ecosystems are nutrient sinks in debt while others are sources, differences that relate to climate, topography and geological history, which leave different parent materials.
Earthworms speed cycling: their bodies add mineral nutrients, their burrowing carries nutrients into mineral soil, and their casts give bacteria and other decomposers access to nutrients.
Organic farms rely on biodiversity to recycle nutrients through soils instead of synthetic fertilizers, but produce sold off the farm opens the cycle and its nutrients may need replacing.
Linnaeus described ecological recycling in 1749, Boussingault showed from 1836 to 1876 that plants need minerals and nitrogen, and in 1872 Ferdinand Cohn described a 'cycle of life'.
The term nutrient cycle appears in an 1899 pamphlet on silviculture, earlier than biogeochemistry, which Vernadsky coined in 1926.

definition.text: A genus of rod-shaped, gram-negative, chemoautotrophic bacteria that oxidize nitrite to nitrate in soil and marine systems.

facts.text: It gets its energy from oxidizing nitrite to nitrate and fixes carbon dioxide through the Calvin cycle; the yield is only −74 kJ per mole of nitrite, so its metabolism is highly specialized.
All members are obligate aerobes with a doubling time of about 13 hours, so oxygen and phosphorus tend to limit their nitrite oxidation.
Widespread in water and soil, it makes nitrate, a primary source of inorganic nitrogen for plants, and grows best at pH 7.3 to 7.5.
Winogradsky isolated pure cultures of nitrifiers in 1890, Warington proposed two-stage nitrification in 1891, and Winogradsky named Nitrobacter in 1892.

conflicts.text: Other sources give a growth optimum at pH 7.9 (Grundmann) or pH optima of 7.6 to 7.8 (Holt).
conflicts.note: Same quantity (optimum growth pH of Nitrobacter); the article itself reports the disagreement between sources.

title: Sulfate-reducing microorganisms

definition.text: Bacteria and archaea that respire anaerobically using sulfate as the terminal electron acceptor, reducing it to hydrogen sulfide.

facts.text: They 'breathe' sulfate instead of oxygen, reducing large amounts for energy and expelling the sulfide (dissimilatory reduction), unlike organisms that reduce a little sulfate to build cell components.
Common in anaerobic environments, they help degrade organic matter by oxidizing the organic acids and alcohols left by fermenting bacteria, competing with acetogens and methanogens.
Their hydrogen sulfide gives salt marshes and mud flats their rotten-egg smell and reacts with metal ions to form insoluble black or brown sulfides such as ferrous sulfide.
They are the dominant source of neurotoxic methylmercury in aquatic systems, and some, able to reduce hydrocarbons, have been used to clean up contaminated soils.

notes: Kept separate from Dissimilatory sulfate reduction (the process, anchored on Sulfur cycle), following the chapter's pattern of Nitrification / Nitrifying bacteria.

definition.text: The movement of oxygen through the Earth's atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and crust.

facts.text: It cycles oxygen atoms between oxidation states in ions, oxides and molecules through redox reactions.
By far the largest store, 99.5% by weight, is the silicate and oxide minerals of the crust and mantle; air, water and life together hold under 0.05%.
Photosynthesis is the main source of free oxygen in the atmosphere.
Free oxygen is lost mainly through respiration and decay, as animals and bacteria consume oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

definition.text: The biogeochemical cycle in which natural and human processes move mercury between chemical forms and environments.

facts.text: Mercury occurs in three oxidation states: 0 (elemental), I (mercurous) and II (mercuric).
Weathering of minerals, geothermal activity and active volcanoes release mercury naturally; cinnabar, a mercury sulfide, is the main ore.
Gold mining, coal burning and copper or lead production are human sources; over 5000 metric tons reach the atmosphere each year.
Bacteria and archaea turn inorganic mercury into methylmercury, which builds up in organisms and concentrates up food chains.

definition.text: The biogeochemical cycle that moves silica, including silica made by living things, between the Earth's systems.

facts.text: Weathering is the main source of silicate on land, at rates set by rainfall, runoff, vegetation, rock type and topography.
Plants take up silicic acid to build phytoliths, rigid structures in their cells that strengthen them and deter herbivores.
Silica released by dissolving phytoliths is estimated at double the rate of global silicate weathering.
Rivers carry silica to the ocean at approximately 6 Tmol Si per year, the main land sink.
400 years of expanding agriculture have exposed more rock and soil, raising silicate weathering and the leaching of amorphous silica from soils.
Through continental weathering the silica cycle overlaps the carbon cycle and helps sequester carbon.

definition.text: The science of the chemical, physical, geological and biological processes that govern the make-up of the natural environment, the pedosphere included.

facts.text: It centres on the biogeochemical cycles of elements and their passage through living things, with particular emphasis on carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur, iron and phosphorus.
Eighteenth-century agricultural interest in soil chemistry improved understanding of nutrients, and an 1844 paper by Dumas and Boussingault is counted a milestone of the field.
Vladimir Vernadsky, whose 1926 book The Biosphere treated the Earth as a living whole, is called the founder of modern biogeochemistry.
A systems science close to systems ecology, it is housed in many disciplines, from ecology, geology and oceanography to soil science.
Its research fields include recovery from soil and water acidification, eutrophication, carbon sequestration, environmental remediation and soil chemistry.
Evolutionary biogeochemistry applies the study of these cycles to Earth's geologic history and the evolution of life.

title: Leghemoglobin

definition.text: An oxygen-carrying plant globin found in the nitrogen-fixing root nodules of legumes.

facts.text: Legumes make it only when their roots are colonised by rhizobia; like hemoglobin, which it closely resembles, it is red.
It keeps free oxygen low enough for oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase to work while holding enough total oxygen for the respiration that energy-hungry nitrogen fixation needs.
Leghemoglobins build up to millimolar levels and buffer free oxygen in the nanomolar range; they are required for symbiotic fixation but not for growth when fixed nitrogen is supplied.
A 1995 study credited low nodule oxygen to low cell permeability, making oxygen delivery its main job; 2005 knockout studies found it both buffers oxygen and delivers it.

contested_note: Studies disagree on whether its main role is buffering free oxygen or delivering oxygen for respiration; a 2005 study supports both.

definition.text: A technique that uses the heavy stable isotope nitrogen-15 to follow and measure conversions within the nitrogen cycle.

facts.text: It separates simultaneous soil processes, such as ammonium being made by mineralisation while being oxidised and assimilated, which bulk concentrations alone cannot explain.
Natural-abundance methods express 15N as delta values relative to air and need no disturbance; the 15N site preference within nitrous oxide helps tell nitrification from denitrification.
Enrichment methods add 15N-labelled ammonium or nitrate, allowing precise rate calculations, though the added nitrogen can itself bias natural transformations.
Rates of simultaneous transformations are solved numerically, for example with the Ntrace model, based on a Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation.

definition.text: A genus of bacteria that oxidises nitrite to nitrate, the second step of nitrification.

facts.text: First described in 1986 from the Gulf of Maine, it lives in forest soils, rice paddies and farmland as well as water systems and wastewater plants.
It is hard to culture, so most of what is known about it comes from molecular and genomic data.
Some members, such as Nitrospira inopinata, carry out complete nitrification (comammox), overturning the long-held view that the two steps need two organisms.
Some split urea with their own urease, and the ammonia they release lets ammonia oxidisers live alongside them.

definition.text: The biological cycle of selenium, in which some organisms reduce its oxidised forms and others oxidise the reduced element back again.

facts.text: Bacteria, fungi and plants, especially species of Astragalus, reduce selenate or selenite to selenide.
Accumulator plants of semi-arid seleniferous soils return organic selenium to the soil when they decay, yet soil selenium there stays mainly inorganic, evidence that it is re-oxidised.
Reduction of selenate to selenite followed by adsorption to clay and reaction with iron locks selenium in sediment; some organic forms volatilise from water, sediment or plants.
Oxidation and methylation by plant roots and microorganisms make selenium available to food chains again.

definition.text: The process by which living organisms build sulfur into their biological molecules.

facts.text: Plant roots take up sulfate actively, at a cost in ATP; the transpiration stream carries it to the shoot, where chloroplasts reduce it to sulfide and build it into cysteine.
Root uptake generally reaches its maximum rate at sulfate levels of 0.1 mM and lower.
When sulfate runs short, most sulfate transporter genes are expressed up to 100-fold more strongly, raising uptake capacity.
Bacteria and fungi follow a similar route, taking up sulfate and reducing it through APS and sulfite to sulfide for cysteine.

title: Urease

definition.text: A nickel-containing enzyme that breaks urea down into carbon dioxide and ammonia.

facts.text: The hydrolysis runs in two stages, through carbamic acid, and the basic ammonia it releases raises the pH around it.
A key catalyst of the nitrogen cycle, it occurs as a soil enzyme, likely because soil microbes gain from the ammonium it frees.
Urea makes up more than half of synthetic nitrogen fertilizer, and because rapid breakdown wastes it, inhibiting urease with chemicals such as NBPT is an agricultural goal.
Environmental urease activity is often measured as an indicator of the health of microbial communities.

notes: Urease was the first enzyme crystallized (S:d2018720028a), shown by Sumner in 1926 to be a protein (S:ffaf41e5e9d7); kept as mentions.

title: Nitrous oxide reductase

definition.text: The enzyme that performs the last step of bacterial denitrification, reducing nitrous oxide to nitrogen gas.

facts.text: Its consumption of nitrous oxide inside cells greatly limits emissions of this potent greenhouse gas to the atmosphere.
Only denitrifying prokaryotes can turn N2O into N2; some communities can do only this step, while some denitrifiers lack it and stop at N2O.
Encoded by nos genes, it is a copper enzyme in the bacterial periplasm whose catalytic CuZ site is a tetranuclear copper-sulfide cluster.
Acetylene is its most specific inhibitor.

notes: Phrase-dossier concept; the page Nitrous-oxide reductase turned out to be crawled, so it is used as the article.
